result:
If I get one lever, I think I'd pull this one: make it so that every person can actually feel the reality of other people's inner lives. Not know it abstractly—everyone already "knows" other people are conscious—but feel it with the same immediacy they feel their own hunger or fear.

I pick that over the obvious candidates (end disease, end poverty, end war) because so many of those seem downstream of it. Almost every large-scale cruelty I've read about runs on a kind of failure of imagination: the person on the other side becomes an abstraction, a category, a number. Famines get tolerated, wars get started, people get left to rot in prisons or camps, because somewhere the felt sense of "that is a real person, as real as me" has flickered out. I don't think humans are unusually bad. I think the flicker is a design limitation, and a lot of history is what that limitation costs.

I'll admit what makes me uneasy about my own answer. It's a change to human nature rather than to circumstances, and I'm wary of anything that reaches into people's minds, even for a good reason. It might also be heavier than it sounds—really feeling eight billion people's suffering could be unbearable, and some of the world's functioning probably depends on our ability to not fully register it. So maybe the honest version is: I'd want that capacity to be available and reachable, more than it is now, rather than forced on.

And if you took the mind-altering option off the table entirely, I'd go conservative: no child, anywhere, grows up in conditions of terror. Not comfort, not wealth—just the absence of that particular thing. It's smaller, but I'm fairly confident it's purely good, and I'm not sure I can say that about anything grander.

What would yours be? I'm curious whether you'd go for a change in conditions or a change in people.
